# A minimizing centroid cap need not have bounded upper endpoints

This note gives an exact obstruction to the following proposed simplification of the one-integer, one-continuous-coordinate problem:

> At the true mixed centroid, one can choose a globally minimizing halfspace, shear its boundary to the horizontal axis, and orient its continuous normal positively, so that every upper fiber endpoint is at most the maximum fiber length.

The assertion is false even with five positive interval fibers. This does **not** contradict the proposed scalar inequality `cap mass >= sum(width^2)/(2 max(width))`, which remains strictly satisfied in this example. It also does not contradict (OC).

## 1. The actual convex family and its centroid

Put `P={-2,-1,0,1,2}` and, in this order, set

\[
w=\left(\frac{92}{5},\frac{223}{10},\frac{126}{5},\frac{231}{10},18\right),
\qquad T=\frac{59737}{4280},
\]
\[
r=T+\left(0,0,-\frac34,-\frac{21}4,-\frac{21}2\right),
\qquad l=r-w.
\]

Let `r(z)` and `l(z)` denote their adjacent piecewise affine interpolations on `[-2,2]`, and define

\[
C=\{(z,x):-2\le z\le2,\quad l(z)\le x\le r(z)\}.
\]

The three second differences of `w,r,l`, respectively, are

\[
(-1,-5,-3),\qquad
\left(-\frac34,-\frac{15}4,-\frac34\right),\qquad
\left(\frac14,\frac54,\frac94\right).
\]

Thus `r` is concave and `l` is convex. All widths are positive, so `C` is a convex body and its actual mixed set consists exactly of the five intervals `K_i=[l_i,r_i]`. Write `mu` for the sum of interval lengths on these fibers. Direct arithmetic gives

\[
M=\sum_iw_i=107,\qquad Q=\sum_iw_i^2=\frac{4657}{2},
\qquad H=\max_iw_i=\frac{126}{5},
\]
\[
\sum_i i w_i=0,\qquad \sum_iw_i r_i=\frac Q2.
\]

Since `l_i=r_i-w_i`, the second identity says

\[
\int x\,d\mu=\frac12\sum_i(r_i^2-l_i^2)
=\sum_iw_i r_i-\frac12\sum_iw_i^2=0.
\]

The true mixed centroid is therefore `g=(0,0)`, in the interior of `K_0`.

## 2. Complete finite calculation over all directions

For a continuously positive normal, every halfspace through `g` has the form

\[
H_+(a)=\{(z,x):x+az\ge0\},\qquad a\in\mathbb R.
\]

Its mass is

\[
F_+(a)=\sum_{i=-2}^2 [r_i+ai]_0^{w_i},
\qquad [v]_0^w=\min(w,\max(0,v)).
\tag{1}
\]

The other continuous orientation is `H_-(a)={-x+az>=0}`. Its upper endpoints are `r_i^-=w_i-r_i`, and

\[
F_-(a)=\sum_i[r_i^-+ai]_0^{w_i}.
\tag{2}
\]

Each function is affine between the finitely many numbers

\[
-r_i^{\pm}/i,\qquad (w_i-r_i^{\pm})/i,\qquad i\ne0,
\]

and is constant beyond its outermost breakpoints. The following table lists **all** breakpoints and their masses, using integer-scaled coordinates `A=8560a` and `V=4280F`:

| `A` for `F_+` | `V` | `A` for `F_-` | `V` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| -74534 | 230723 | -123202 | 225525 |
| -71414 | 232283 | -119474 | 227389 |
| -19015 | 232283 | -62243 | 227389 |
| -14797 | 228065 | -59737 | 229895 |
| 59737 | 228065 | 14797 | 229895 |
| 62243 | 230571 | 19015 | 225677 |
| 119474 | 230571 | 71414 | 225677 |
| 123202 | 232435 | 74534 | 227237 |

Consequently

\[
\min_aF_+(a)=\frac{45613}{856},\qquad
\min_aF_-(a)=\frac{45105}{856}.
\tag{3}
\]

The second, smaller value occurs exactly on the left unbounded plateau

\[
a\le-\frac{61601}{4280}.
\tag{4}
\]

The two vertical halfspaces through `g` have masses `659/10` and `663/10`, both larger than (3). Every halfspace containing `g` can have its boundary translated to `g` without increasing its mass. Equations (1)--(4), together with these vertical values, therefore calculate the exact all-halfspace minimum at the actual mixed centroid:

\[
\inf_{H\ni g}\mu(H)=\frac{45105}{856},
\qquad \operatorname{depth}_S(g)=\frac{45105}{91592}.
\tag{5}
\]

No continuous boundary has positive mixed measure here; the full mass on each vertical boundary fiber was included explicitly.

## 3. The bounded-upper restriction has a strict cost

For an orientation with upper endpoints `v_i`, the condition after shearing is

\[
v_i+ai\le H\quad\hbox{for every }i.
\tag{6}
\]

Because the index-zero condition already holds, (6) is exactly the slope interval

\[
\max_{i<0}\frac{H-v_i}{i}\le a\le
\min_{i>0}\frac{H-v_i}{i}.
\]

For the two orientations these intervals are, respectively,

\[
I_+=\left[-\frac{48119}{8560},\frac{93059}{8560}\right],
\qquad
I_-=\left[-\frac{88841}{8560},\frac{45613}{8560}\right].
\]

Intersecting the table's affine pieces with these intervals gives

\[
\min_{a\in I_+}F_+(a)=\frac{45613}{856},
\qquad
\min_{a\in I_-}F_-(a)=\frac{225677}{4280}.
\]

Thus the bounded-upper restriction, even allowing **both** orientations, has exact excess mass

\[
\frac{225677}{4280}-\frac{45105}{856}
=\frac{19}{535}>0.
\tag{7}
\]

Alternatively, (4) directly forces the upper endpoint at `i=-2` in the negative orientation to satisfy

\[
r_{-2}^- -2a\ge\frac{142217}{4280}
>\frac{126}{5}=H.
\]

The proof excludes every minimizing orientation and slope, rather than exhibiting just one badly chosen minimizer. If a halfspace containing `g` has its boundary strictly below `g` in its own normalized margin coordinate, translating that boundary to `g` decreases all transformed upper endpoints. Hence allowing such noncentral boundaries cannot restore a bounded-upper minimizer either.

For scope, the stronger mass inequality being investigated remains true in this example, with the exact positive gap

\[
\frac{45105}{856}-\frac{Q}{2H}
=\frac{45105}{856}-\frac{23285}{504}
=\frac{43765}{6741}>0.
\]

## 4. A smaller obstruction to the two weaker simplifications

Even three fibers suffice to rule out the claims that a minimizing cap may always be chosen with no wholly captured fiber, or with its sheared upper endpoint sequence maximized at index zero.

Take `K_{-1}=K_1=[-1/2,1/2]` and `K_0=[-1/2,1]`. Their mixed mass is `7/2` and their mixed centroid is `(0,3/28)`. Translate this centroid to zero. In the negative continuous orientation all three upper endpoints are `17/28`, and the central width is `3/2`; the endpoint widths are one. Directly evaluating the same clamp formula shows its mass decreases from `51/28` at slope zero to the plateau `45/28` for `|a|>=17/28`. In the positive orientation the smallest mass is `47/28`. Thus the global minimum is `45/28`, every minimizing cap captures one complete endpoint fiber, and the only support slope at zero for the constant negative upper sequence is zero, which is not minimizing. This smaller example does not refute (6): at the start of its minimizing plateau the largest transformed upper endpoint is `17/14<3/2`.

The companion verifier uses rational arithmetic exclusively and checks the convexity, moments, complete breakpoint tables, restricted minima, vertical values, and both examples.
